inline.s: One who recites the Buddha's name should above all understand this principle. You must know that when Amitābha comes to welcome you, he has never actually come; and when you are reborn in the West, you have never actually gone. Yet although there is in truth neither coming nor going, what harm is there in coming and going appearing? Why is this? The absence of coming and going is the substance of principle; the presence of coming and going is the mark of affairs. Principle and affairs have never been two, and nature and marks must be perfectly interfused. Therefore, although there is no coming and going, this does not hinder there being coming and going; and although there is coming and going, in truth there is no coming and going. What matters most is this: coming and going must be realized upon non-coming and non-going, and non-coming and non-going is accomplished precisely in the midst of coming and going. This is the essential secret of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth. Gain this secret, and you will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land, and certainly see the Buddha. Who says that one who cultivates the Pure Land need not study prajñā, or doubts that prajñā obstructs the Pure Land?

There is a further essential point that must be thoroughly understood. Marks arise depending on nature; nature is revealed through marks. Nature and marks, the one outward and the other inward, are never apart from each other. Why, then, do the Buddhist scriptures tell people to be apart from marks? You should understand that what is called being apart does not mean annihilation, but only that one should not grasp.

Now nature and marks, being the one outward and the other inward, cannot be separated. Why, then, should marks alone not be grasped? You should understand that this is because ordinary beings, from beginningless time, have known only how to identify with marks and to turn along with them. Thus the various opposing marks of self and other, this and that, high and low, thick and thin, fine and coarse, fair and foul, rise up one after another in profusion, pulling in branch and leaf until they draw in more and more. As a result, discrimination and clinging grow daily more severe, and the view of self grows daily deeper. The afflictions of greed, anger, and the rest of the three poisons go on ever increasing. So it reaches the point of endless karma-making and boundless suffering.

Now if we wish to save ourselves from this, we must cut off the three poisons. To cut off the three poisons, we must rid ourselves of the view of self. To rid ourselves of the view of self, we must not discriminate or cling. And to be free of discriminating and clinging, we must be apart from marks. Therefore, when it is said that one should be apart from marks, the meaning is that one should rid oneself of the self-view that consists in discrimination and clinging. It does not mean being apart from them once and for all. Hence the text says, "One should not grasp the marks of non-Dharma," and again, "One should not speak of marks of annihilation." This is precisely to reveal the true meaning of being apart from marks, so that it will not be misunderstood.

In short, being apart from marks is for the sake of turning the light around and shining within, so as to realize the nature. Once the nature is realized, marks should then rightly be manifested. But if one would, after realizing the fruit, not sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, one must also, while cultivating the cause, contemplate emptiness without leaning to emptiness. This is why the text instructs one neither to grasp nor to annihilate, so that one does not settle on either extreme.

Moreover, Buddhist principle and the Buddha's teaching are in every way perfect and sublime. Though he speaks only of not grasping marks, in fact this already reaches through to the nature. How is this so? The moment there is grasping, it becomes a mark and is no longer the nature. Hence the Two Vehicles leaned to the side of nature, and the Buddha reproached them, saying: they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, and have not been able to see the nature. To say "sink" and to say "stagnate" is to describe the very mark of their grasping. When the mark of sinking and stagnation appears, the nature that does not sink or stagnate is hidden. Hence he says they have not seen the nature. Therefore the one phrase "not grasping marks" runs through both extremes, and should be understood in this way.

As for this passage, it does not say there is coming and going, nor does it say there is no coming and going. It only says, "Nowhere does it come from, and nowhere does it go." Illuminating both extremes at once, it is especially perfectly interfused. Why is this? If one were to assert definitely that there is coming and going, one would lean to the side of marks. If one were to assert definitely that there is no coming and going, one would lean to the side of no-marks. To speak here by illuminating both extremes at once is precisely to reveal the meaning that nature and marks are mutually interfused. When nature and marks are mutually interfused, this is equality and oneness. Again, the name Tathāgata, though it is used to designate the dharmakāya, in fact already contains the other bodies as well; otherwise the word "come" would have nothing to refer to. Thus this very name is enough to make plain that although there are three, they are not three separate substances. Above, the meaning was explained in terms of the word "thus," so that it extended to the side of all dharmas, and it was said that all dharmas are thus. Here the meaning is explained in terms of the word "come," so that it extends to the side of neither coming nor going, and it is said that it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. These are all the World-Honored One's earnest, heartfelt instructions, teaching students that all the dharmas spoken by the Buddha should be understood in this way. Then one can penetrate the oneness of nature and marks and the equality of the dharma-realm.

Why is this? If one understands that although there is neither coming nor going, coming and going nonetheless appear, one knows that the dharmakāya constantly manifests the reward body, the transformation body, and the rest without ever ceasing. Therefore, while cultivating the cause, one should not annihilate marks. If one understands that although coming and going appear, in truth there is never any coming and going, one knows that the reward body, the transformation body, and the rest cannot exist apart from the dharmakāya. Therefore, while cultivating the cause, one should not cling to marks. Understand this, and all that was said before — that one should not grasp dharmas, should not grasp non-dharmas, and that "is not" and "is named" — can be thoroughly and completely understood.

And the meaning that if one sees all marks as no-marks, one then sees the Tathāgata, is likewise penetrated through this. For "thus come" means not annihilating marks; "come thus" means not clinging to marks. And "if one sees all marks as no-marks" means that in the very midst of marks one sees them as no-marks; this is precisely not clinging and not annihilating, and so it accords with the meaning of Tathāgata. Therefore one can see the Tathāgata.

Moreover, "thus come" means that even while not clinging, one does not annihilate; "come thus" means that even while not annihilating, one still does not cling. Therefore not dwelling in nirvāṇa and not dwelling in birth-and-death are simultaneous. It is a dwelling in nothing at all. Hence the practitioner should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere; if the mind dwells anywhere, then it does not truly dwell. If one can thus understand and penetrate this, then nature, marks, all discrimination, and all clinging will of themselves dissolve. Of themselves there will be no thought. Of themselves there will be no hindrance or inversion. Hence it is said: when one practices the profound prajñā-pāramitā, one can cross over all suffering. If practitioners grasp the meaning of this section, they should contemplate that all the marks of opposition cannot exist apart from the absolutely unrelated nature, nor does the absolutely unrelated nature ever exist apart from the marks of opposition. In all the affairs and marks of opposition in daily life, though one may follow conditions in one's actions, one must not be turned about by conditions. The meaning is this: when a condition should be resolved, resolve it as soon as the opportunity comes, without entanglement; when a condition should be formed, there is no harm in forming it, but do not go seeking conditions. If one can truly be thus, diligently contemplating and closely examining oneself throughout the day and night, holding the mind steady and planting the feet firmly, one will of oneself not be bound by marks, and will dissolve marks and enter the substance. This is the student's foremost task. It is according with true suchness. It is pointing directly upward.

As for what is called dissolving marks: "dissolve" means to blend, not to annihilate; it is neither clinging nor cutting off. As for what is called entering the substance: it means realizing and entering the substance of the nature. When marks are blended, that is realizing the substance; there is no separate substance to enter. Why is this? The substance of the nature is fundamentally without marks and yet not without marks. This is what is called the empty mark of all dharmas. This emptiness is emptiness in the primary sense, which is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty. It means emptying only the marks without destroying the dharmas. If one can be thus, then though ten thousand marks come crowding in, one is of oneself unmoved by them. All that has been said above is the skillful means for cultivating practice that begins from this empty mark of all dharmas. There are deep and shallow levels, and the methods are not uniform, yet they can still be threaded into one. Moreover, what is called shallow is not shallow without depth, and one should not slight it because it seems shallow. Let those who have the affinity take it up and practice it as they see fit. There is great benefit in it; it will certainly not deceive you.

blocks.text: The Unity of Marks, Part Thirty

inline.s: (Gui) Next, explaining detachment from oneness and multiplicity in terms of dust-motes and worlds. This is divided into two: (Zi) first, explaining that dust-motes are not many; next, explaining that the world is not one. (Zi) The first is again divided into three: (Chou) first, asking whether dust-motes are many; next, explaining that many is not many; third, explaining the reason why.
(Chou) First, asking whether dust-motes are many.
"Subhūti, if a good man or good woman were to reduce the three-thousand great thousandfold world to dust-motes, what do you think? Would the multitude of those dust-motes be many?"

Dust-motes and worlds have been spoken of before, it is true. But in this section the emphasis falls on the two words "reduce" and "gather." Because they can be reduced and can be gathered, this is enough to prove that the marks of dust-motes and worlds all arise from conditions and are empty just as they are. And in the dharma-nature there are fundamentally none of these various distinctions of marks (read in the departing tone). Therefore, although they are not annihilated, they must not be clung to. Now, the earlier teaching repeatedly said "is not" and "is named," but it only stated that marks are so and nature is so as a matter of course. Here, in terms of dust-motes and worlds, it explains that they can be reduced and gathered, and so it explains the reason why thoroughly. Once this meaning is clear, all places where it says "is not" and "is named" can be understood by analogy.

To reduce the three-thousand great thousandfold world to dust-motes — this one phrase is enough to awaken the deluded ordinary being and warn him not to cling to the world as truly existing. Why is this? That so vast a world can be reduced is proof enough that the world is a mark of illusion; how could it truly exist? If it truly existed, how could it be reduced? What is called "reduce" makes clear that the world is a mark formed by the convergence of countless dust-motes. Apart from dust-motes, there is no other world. One who has resolved for bodhi should contemplate in this way: every world is nothing but dust-motes, and must not be clung to as truly existing. This does not mean actually pounding it to pieces. When the text above says "good man or good woman," it is referring to those who have resolved for bodhi.

"What do you think?" is a phrase testing and probing one's level of insight. If one knows that the multitude of dust-motes comes from the world being reduced, then it is clear that the world is a provisional existent. But if one clings to there being a multitude, then one has again mistaken dust-motes for truly existing things. You should understand that worlds and dust-motes, though they differ in size, are one in being unreal. The Buddha speaks of reducing a world into motes because he wishes to break people's view that the world truly exists. If the unreality of the motes is not made clear, then the unreality of the world can never be made thoroughly clear. For the World-Honored One's original intent is to have people thoroughly understand that everything in the world, from the greatest world down to the smallest dust-mote, is nothing but illusion, empty just as it is, not to be clung to and not to be coveted. Hence he must test and probe one's level of insight. The word "reduce" here and the word "gather" below, the word "multitude" here and the word "one" below, stand far apart and face each other. These are precisely the eye of the text, and they are meant to make one grasp the true meaning right here.
(Chou) Next, explaining that many is not many.
"Very many, World-Honored One. Why is this? If the multitude of dust-motes truly existed, the Buddha would not have spoken of a multitude of dust-motes."

In the popular editions, the words "Subhūti said" precede "very many"; the ancient editions do not have them. The answer "very many" is spoken with reference to the illusory marks of dust-motes, and it also shows that he has already been able to understand that the world is not truly existing. A single world is nothing but many dust-motes — how could a world truly exist? It further shows that he can also understand that dust-motes too are not truly existing. The words following "why is this?" explain this meaning. The sense is that the World-Honored One first said that the world is reduced to dust-motes, and then, when testing his level of insight, spoke of "a multitude of dust-motes," deliberately adding the word "multitude." "Multitude" means a convergence. It is then clear that dust-motes too are an illusory mark of convergence. How then do they differ from the world, which is an illusory mark formed by convergence? So one can know that they too are not truly existing. Hence it says: if the multitude of dust-motes truly existed, the Buddha would not have spoken of a multitude of dust-motes. From this it can be seen that the answer "very many" is precisely what brings out that they are an illusory mark of convergence. Hence it is said: the answer "very many" is spoken with reference to illusory marks.

You should understand that when a world is reduced to dust, who could fail to know that the number is vast? Why need it be asked? This shows that the point of the question lies in the word "multitude." And this meaning was exactly what the Elder saw through — this is what is called mind answering to mind. This is why he was the fitting vessel in the prajñā assembly, and why he could teach the bodhisattvas on the Buddha's behalf.

When the ancient worthies tested their students, they often deliberately set up such ambushes, and this is the same idea. Why are dust-motes a mark of convergence? It is said that one dust-mote can be analyzed into seven extremely subtle dust-motes, and one extremely subtle dust-mote can be analyzed into seven neighboring-void dust-motes. "Void" means empty; "neighboring-void" is like saying, in modern terms, equal to zero. Hence dust-motes are an illusory mark of convergence and not truly existing. Why did the Elder not simply state this meaning straight out, but instead had to bring out its unreality through the word "multitude"? There is a deep reason here, twofold:

(1) Because since the Buddha had spoken thus, he relied on that to make the meaning clear. To make the meaning clear in reliance on the Buddha's words is to teach those who read the scriptures and hear the Dharma that every word the Buddha spoke is replete with essential meaning. One should listen attentively and not overlook a single word.

(2) The non-Buddhist teachers of the Buddha's time would always analyze the things of the world layer by layer until they reached the indivisible, and still hold it to be truly existing — just like today's chemists. They analyze the various things of the world into a number of elements; what was at first indivisible becomes divisible again after a long while. The work of analysis grows finer with time, until they arrive at so-called atoms and electrons, and still they cling to them as truly existing. The Two Vehicles are not like this. Knowing that a dust-mote can be analyzed into neighboring-void dust-motes, they know that all is empty. Yet they must wait for analysis before they believe it is empty, and so they fall short of the Mahāyāna's ability to contemplate things as empty in their very substance. Now the Elder wished to make clear that dust-motes are not real, and he did not cite the teaching of neighboring-void dust-motes, but instead brought out the meaning through the Buddha's word "multitude." By this he made clear that whatever is formed by convergence is thereby known to be empty and must not be clung to as real. This is why the Buddha's way is utterly different from that of the non-Buddhists. And since one knows it simply by observing the principle, without waiting for analysis, this is why the Mahāyāna is utterly different from the Two Vehicles. The words following "why is this so?" precisely make this meaning clear.
(Chou) Third, explaining the reason why.
"Why is this? What the Buddha speaks of as a multitude of dust-motes is not a multitude of dust-motes; therefore it is named a multitude of dust-motes."

The meaning of this section is as if to say: since the Buddha speaks of it as a multitude of dust-motes, one may know that dust-motes are dharmas arising from conditions. A dharma that arises from conditions is empty just as it is, and is nothing but an illusory mark. This is the reason why dust-motes are not truly existing. "Is not" makes clear, in terms of the one such dharma-nature, that they are fundamentally empty; "is named" makes clear, in terms of the marks of dharmas that arise from conditions, that they are not without a provisional name. To say "the Buddha speaks" is precisely to show that the wisdom of enlightenment shines through: the dharma-nature is fundamentally empty and the marks of dharmas are all illusory — why should one wait for analysis at all? In short, to reduce is to gather, and that is called gathering; to gather is to scatter, and that is called reducing. This is fundamentally an illusory mark formed by opposition. Therefore, at the very moment it exists, it is already empty. Small as dust-motes are, they can be gathered and can be reduced — existence is emptiness, and so it is. Then the world, being great, can be known as well. Hence below the text again speaks in terms of what is great. The Buddha first said that a world can be reduced to dust, and then brought up the dust and asked about its multitude. He meant precisely for people to awaken to the great through the small. Since dust-motes are fundamentally empty, one can by analogy know that all worlds are empty.

(Zi) Next, explaining that the world is not one. This is divided into three: (Chou) first, explaining that what is not a world is named a world; next, explaining that one is not one; third, showing that it is fundamentally apart from verbal expression.
(Chou) First, explaining that what is not a world is named a world.
"World-Honored One, the three-thousand great thousandfold world spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; therefore it is named a world."

This section follows from the sense of the question above. Since the question above said that what is not a world becomes dust, and the Elder then explained that what is not dust becomes empty, it can be known that a world is precisely emptiness. Hence it says, "is not a world; therefore it is named a world." The reason is set out in detail in the section below.

Here the text does not say "the Buddha speaks" but "the Tathāgata speaks," and there is a deep meaning in this. The three-thousand great thousandfold world is called the realm of the transformation body's teaching, because this realm is what all living beings rely upon. The Tathāgata of the dharmakāya, in order to benefit all living beings, follows the conditions of living beings and manifests a transformation body in order to teach and transform them. He never dwells or clings to this realm at all. Why is this? The Tathāgata's dharmakāya pervades the dharma-realm. The dharma-realm is equal to empty space. How could there be any such thing as a three-thousand great thousandfold world? Hence he brings up the Tathāgata and says that the world is not real but is only named. To speak in this way is precisely to open and show living beings that they should contemplate the world as not real and merely named, and so not cling to it. If one does not cling to the world, then one does not cling to anything at all. By such non-clinging, the dharmakāya that is inherently present can emerge from its obstructions. This is the deep meaning of not saying "the Buddha speaks" but saying "the Tathāgata speaks."
(Chou) Next, explaining that one is not one.
"Why is this? If the world truly existed, it would be a unity. What the Tathāgata speaks of as a unity is not a unity; therefore it is named a unity."

The popular editions read "if the world truly exists"; Liu's edition does not have the word "if." Hui's edition reads "if the world has reality." "Has reality" and "truly exists" are in meaning no different. Here we follow Liu's edition, because the corrected editions all follow Liu's edition. "A unity" means that which is gathered into one — equivalent to what we now call a whole. Now those who cling to marks, though they may hear that a world can be reduced to dust, may still think that although it is not truly existing, still, while it is unreduced, its mark of being gathered into one is plainly there. Why is this? A world is originally a collective name. Once a collective name is established, it is the mark of a unity. To block this clinging, the Elder thoroughly refutes it. The sense is: just now you said "is not a world; therefore it is named a world" — why? Because whatever belongs to names and marks is nothing but illusion; hence "is not." "Is not" means that a world is merely a provisional name and not truly existing. It is not only because it can be reduced that we know it is not truly existing; even unreduced, it is still not truly existing. Why? A thousand times four continents is called a small thousandfold world. A thousand times a small thousandfold world is called a middling thousandfold world. A thousand times a middling thousandfold world is called a great thousandfold world. Thus one can see that the name and mark of a world fundamentally has no fixed range. Not only can what is gathered be reduced; the gathering can further gather. How could one cling to a fixed mark of unity? Hence it says, "is not a unity; therefore it is named a unity." This says that it is no more than a provisional name and fundamentally unreal. It makes clear that only if something were truly existing would it be a unity. Now that a unity has no fixed character, to observe the name and mark of a world is enough to prove that it is not truly existing. Why must one wait for the world to be reduced to dust, and the dust reduced to emptiness? Thus the world's being empty just as it is becomes exceedingly plain.
(Chou) Third, showing that it is fundamentally apart from verbal expression.
"Subhūti, a unity is in fact inexpressible, yet ordinary beings are attached to the matter."

Reading the section above on "not many," one can know that the name "gathering" arises only because it can be reduced, and one also knows that what is reduced can be reduced yet further. Then the meaning that all dharmas are empty by nature is clear. Reading the section on "not one," one can know that the name "reducing" arises only because there is gathering, and one also knows that what is gathered can be gathered yet further. Then the meaning that all dharmas arise from conditions is clear. Moreover, viewed as gathering, although it is empty by nature, this does not hinder dependent arising; and because it is dependently arisen, one knows it is empty by nature. It follows that what is called a unity is a oneness that is not fixed as one, a gathering that is not fixed as gathering. Hence it says: a unity is in fact inexpressible. It is inexpressible because a world can be reduced and dust-motes can also be reduced, so that dust-motes are seen to be no different from a world. If one said that a world is truly a unity, would that not make dust-motes truly a unity as well? Yet a world is not a world but dust-motes; and moreover dust-motes are not dust-motes but fundamentally empty. From this one can know that the unity of a world is likewise fundamentally empty. Is this not a case of one being precisely not one, and gathering being precisely not gathering? This is to explain, in terms of marks, that one cannot definitively say it is not a unity, nor definitively say it truly is a unity; hence it is inexpressible.

Now cultivation is fundamentally for the sake of realizing the nature. What was made clear above — that one is not one and gathering is not gathering — is said in terms of the marks of opposing affairs. In terms of the pure nature, none of these things exist at all. Why is this? The nature is absolute, not relative; it is fundamentally apart from the marks of names and the marks of verbal expression. This explains, in terms of the nature, that the nature is not the marks of affairs and is fundamentally apart from verbal expression; hence it is inexpressible.

"Ordinary" means the ordinary sentiment. To be deluded about the marks of affairs is called the ordinary sentiment. Hence it says: ordinary beings are attached to the matter. "The matter" refers broadly to all marks of affairs, and the unity is included within it. To say "are attached" makes clear that they seek outwardly and turn their backs on enlightenment to join with dust. And to speak of the ordinary sentiment makes clear that it is not right knowing. Because they seek outwardly, they give rise to covetous attachment toward the marks of affairs and so produce clinging. It follows that if one wishes not to be attached, one must purify the ordinary sentiment; and to purify the ordinary sentiment, one must open right knowing — this is clear.

How then should one know? One should know that a unity is precisely inexpressible. That is to say, one should be apart from names and verbal expression and turn the light back to see that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn. Thus this section's instruction on the way to enter the path is exceedingly intimate and direct, and must not be taken as mere empty talk about principle.

Moreover, this meaning runs through both what precedes and what follows. The section above, on "coming from nowhere and going nowhere, and therefore named Tathāgata," and the section below, on "the view of self is not the view of self, therefore it is named the view of self," should both be grasped at the point of the inexpressible, and one should not be attached to the matter. Only thus can one truly understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata, and only thus can one accord with and enter the mind-source in which all dharmas are fundamentally unborn. Hence this section precisely answers to the section below that concludes with non-arising, echoing it closely.

The two sections above, on "not many" and "not one," break not only the world but also dust-motes. Here, when it speaks of ordinary beings' attachment, it speaks only in terms of the unity, so it discusses only the world and not dust-motes. Why? There are two meanings here:

(1) The statement above that dust-motes are not truly existing brought out the meaning through the word "multitude." This shows that not only is the world an illusory mark of unity, but dust-motes too are an illusory mark of unity. Hence the inexpressible unity spoken of here refers to both the world and dust-motes together. It is not that dust-motes are left unspoken, nor that only the world is spoken of. This is why the Buddha does not mention world and dust-motes separately but brings up the single unity to speak of it. This should be understood in this way.

(2) To bring up only the unity is intended to refute the notion that nothing in the world, whether great as a world or small as a dust-mote, is other than a false gathering. For the attachment of ordinary beings is nothing but the mistake of taking the marks of false gathering to be real. If this is so of dust and worlds, it is so of the physical body as well. The reason ordinary beings are attached to the stinking skin-bag and cling to it as self is nothing else: it is because they do not know that it is a false gathering of the five aggregates. If they knew that apart from the five aggregates there is no such physical body, they would not become attached. This is the subtle intent behind the Buddha's bringing up only the unity. For in breaking the dependent retribution, he breaks the primary retribution as well. This should be understood in this way.
This major section, explaining detachment from oneness and multiplicity in terms of dust-motes and worlds, contains a great breadth of meaning. Let me now set it out in several parts.

(1) Since dust-motes and worlds are neither one nor many, it can be seen that they are also neither whole nor particular. For at first glance a world is a whole mark and dust-motes are particular marks. Because a world is a whole mark, one mistakenly takes it to be truly a unity; because dust-motes are particular marks, one does not know that they too are false gatherings. In fact, since a world can be reduced, the whole is not whole; and since dust-motes too are false gatherings, the particular is not particular.

(2) To say neither one nor many is to say neither increasing nor decreasing. For in terms of volume, the mark of a world seems to increase while the mark of dust-motes seems to decrease; yet in terms of number, the mark of a world seems to decrease while the mark of dust-motes seems to increase. Thus increase and decrease have no fixed mark; they too are provisional names and illusions. Indeed, increase and decrease are both inexpressible. Hence it says, "neither increasing nor decreasing." The phrase "neither increasing nor decreasing" means that increase and decrease are inexpressible. Other phrases such as "neither arising nor ceasing" carry the same meaning. In short, once one understands that a world is not a world and dust is not dust, one suddenly sees that all the opposing names and marks in the world — great and small, high and low, coming and going, one and many, whole and particular, increasing and decreasing, wise and foolish, pure and impure — are nothing but illusion and are empty just as they are. If one understands that all dharmas are fundamentally empty, one will return to the nature and all dharmas will be one such. And so dharmas are equal. This is the essential meaning of the empty mark of all dharmas. Grasp this meaning, and one can contemplate everything in this way. When the power of contemplation is mature, one can realize the patient acceptance of non-arising and dissolve marks to enter the substance. This must not go unknown.

(3) The section above on detachment from coming and going explained, in terms of the three bodies, the meaning that the nature is empty and yet dependent arising occurs. Coming and going is dependent arising; neither coming nor going is emptiness of nature. That was explained in terms of the primary retribution. Once the Buddha's primary retribution is clear, then the primary retribution of all living beings should be contemplated in the same way. This section on detachment from oneness and multiplicity explains, in terms of dust-motes and worlds, the meaning that the nature is empty and yet dependent arising occurs. Dust-motes and worlds are not dust-motes and worlds: that is emptiness of nature. They are named dust-motes and worlds: that is dependent arising. This is explained in terms of the dependent retribution. The great thousandfold world is the realm of one Buddha's teaching, and also the realm on which the physical bodies of all living beings rely. If the realm on which the physical body relies is named yet not real, then all the marks of affairs arising from this body and this realm should be contemplated in the same way.

Why is this so? The primary retribution and the dependent retribution are what living beings cannot be parted from even for a moment, and even these are illusory and unreal. Then all the opposing marks of affairs — prosperity and decline, suffering and joy, praise and ridicule, defamation and renown — are all the more illusory and unreal. How could they be worth coveting? This is the subtle intent with which the scripture explains the empty mark of all dharmas in terms of the three bodies and the world. Why? Because by explaining the meaning through these two, all marks of affairs are comprehensively included without remainder.

(4) In terms of the marks of body and realm, the body is what relies and the realm is what is relied upon. But in terms of the holy one's dharma-body and the ordinary being's Buddha-nature, the nature is what brings forth, and body and realm are what are brought forth. You should understand that this pure nature fundamentally has no coming and going, no oneness and multiplicity, no whole and particular, no increase and decrease; it merely manifests, in accord with conditions, the marks of coming and going and so on. Because marks arise in accord with conditions, they are illusory; whereas the nature is the inherently present and real substance. Therefore, although it manifests in accord with conditions all the various opposing marks of affairs, within the intrinsically absolute, empty, and still nature there have never been any of those various marks. So it is with all other marks as well: one and different, holy and ordinary, arising and ceasing, defiled and pure, self and other, this and that.

If one can truly fix one's gaze in a single glance upon the mind-source that is fundamentally unborn, and contemplate one's way into it, this is what is called pointing directly upward. Then the heart opens out on the spot, afflictions vanish on the spot, and inversion and dreaming are left far behind on the spot. To work in this way is truly to take it up directly, and one may be called a person who works well. Compared with those who do it twig by twig and joint by joint, the difference in effectiveness is what the ancients called a day against a kalpa — and not merely a thousand miles a day.

Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Knowing illusion, one is at once apart from it, without resorting to skillful means. Being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and living beings of the final age who cultivate in accordance with this can thus forever be apart from all illusions." What this passage of scripture says can serve precisely as a footnote to our own sutra. It is exactly the practice of pointing directly upward.

How does one cultivate? Knowing illusion, one is at once apart from it; being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened. That is it. "Knowing" means understanding, that is, enlightened contemplation. "Illusion" means what was said above: body, world, and so on, which are named yet not real. How is one at once apart from it? Fix the gaze in a single glance upon the mind-source and contemplate one's way into it, and all illusions are at once left behind. For to know illusion is already to be apart from it. To contemplate with such enlightenment is to accord with enlightenment. Therefore to be apart from illusion is already to be awakened. This is the essential gate of the perfect and sudden teaching, entering directly in one leap — what gradual stages are there? Among all Dharma-doors, none is more skillful than this. Why resort to further skillful means? Looking at the words "thus can one forever be apart from all illusions," one can know that only such cultivation is thorough and reaches the ultimate. Those who hear this should give rise to the thought that it is rare and hard to encounter.

(5) There is, moreover, another meaning set out by the bodhisattva Asaṅga, which should also be known. What is that meaning? It takes the section on dust-motes and worlds being neither one nor many as a simile to illustrate the meaning of the section above. The oneness of a world illustrates that the reward body is one. The multiplicity of dust-motes illustrates that the transformation bodies are many. Dust-motes and worlds being neither one nor many illustrates that the two bodies are neither one nor different. But there is a point where the illustration and the Dharma do not match: a world does not exist apart from dust-motes, but the reward body is not such that apart from the transformation bodies it would not exist. You should understand that any simile can illustrate only the general outline, not match point for point. For instance, the scriptures often use sunlight to illustrate the light of wisdom. This is only because among the lights of the world sunlight is the greatest, the most pervasive, and the most beneficial, and so it is taken as a simile. In fact, sunlight arises depending on form and substance, and it is hot; how could it compare with the light of wisdom, which depends on nothing at all and is moreover cool? Therefore one must not, because of Asaṅga's explanation and the mismatch between illustration and Dharma, make light of it. Dust-motes and worlds presently having oneness and multiplicity illustrates the two bodies presently having coming and going; yet in terms of nature, there is fundamentally no mark of oneness or multiplicity, and hence also no mark of coming or going. And speaking in terms of nature and marks together: although fundamentally there is no oneness or multiplicity, it does not hinder oneness and multiplicity appearing; and although oneness and multiplicity appear, in truth there is still no oneness or multiplicity. This illustrates that although fundamentally there is no coming or going, it does not hinder coming and going appearing; and although coming and going appear, in truth there is no coming or going. But ordinary beings are attached to the marks of the unity, which illustrates that ordinary beings are attached to the marks of coming and going. Asaṅga's treatise says: "In order to break the name-and-form body, therefore worlds, dust-motes, and the rest are spoken of." "Name-and-form body" means the two bodies. The sense is that the Buddha feared people would not understand the meaning above, and so spoke further of the simile of worlds and dust-motes to break through it. Now I explain and draw out this meaning at length so that those who read his treatise may be able to reconcile and grasp it. From this it can be seen that when the Buddha speaks one sentence of Dharma it contains measureless meanings, and so it can be given all kinds of interpretations. This is why it is called the perfect voice. Hence those of shallow or deep insight each follow their own capacity. Through the ages there have been many who studied the perfect and sudden great teaching and yet ended by expounding it as the separate teaching, and some even fell into the teaching of gods and humans; the reason lies here. Hence it is said that ghee can turn into poison, and also that when a perfect person speaks the Dharma, no Dharma is not perfect. When a perverse person meets the true Dharma, the true Dharma too becomes perverse. Therefore the Mahāyāna scriptures teach students that drawing near to good friends is the essential enterprise and opening right views is the foundation.

blocks.text: Non-Arising of Knowing and Seeing, Part Thirty-One

inline.s: (Gui) Third, explaining, in terms of the view of self, that detachment too is to be detached from. This is divided into two: (Zi) first, clarifying the meaning by question and answer; next, explaining and establishing the reason.
(Zi) First, clarifying the meaning by question and answer.

"Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha speaks of a view of self, a view of a person, a view of a being, and a view of a life — Subhūti, what do you think? Would such a person understand the meaning I have spoken?" "World-Honored One, such a person would not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata."

In the popular editions, the two characters "No, indeed" are added after "World-Honored One"; they should not be there. Hence they are absent from the Tang dynasty written scriptures. Just look at the words "would not understand" below — how resolute they are. How could a lively phrase like "No, indeed" be added before them? If it were not a lively phrase but a dead one, it would not only be inconsistent with the meaning above; the one phrase "would not understand" is already sufficient to make the meaning plain. Why need a dead phrase like "No, indeed" to make the meaning clear? You should understand that this sutra has not one superfluous sentence or superfluous word. From this alone one knows that those who recklessly add "No, indeed" wholly fail to understand the purport of the sutra.

The meaning of this section is extremely profound. Why? Everything spoken throughout the sutra is for the sake of breaking the self. Why, then, would someone who says the Buddha speaks of a view of self fail to understand the meaning? Some may say: this person suspects that the Buddha, in speaking these words, must have had this view in mind, and hence it says he does not understand. This explanation is very wrong. No matter who it is, no one would suspect the Buddha of having a view of self. Even if there really were such a deluded person harboring this deluded doubt, then after "if someone were to say" there should be a sentence saying "the Buddha had this thought." But there is none, which proves the explanation wrong.

How then does he fail to understand? You should understand that from the opening of the sutra onward, it has repeatedly said that the four marks of self, person, being, and life must not be present, and that one who has them is not a bodhisattva. It has also praised those who are free of these four marks as gaining measureless merit. It further has the bodhisattva penetrate the selfless Dharma. And it says: to know that all dharmas are selfless and attain patient acceptance — such merit is supreme. But it feared that ordinary beings, hearing the Buddha repeat this again and again, would come to hold that the view of self and the rest truly exist. Once this view is lodged in the mind, that is precisely the view of self. Would this not add to their bonds? And even if they did not do so, but could gradually rid themselves of the self, that too would not be the meaning of the Buddha's speaking this profound prajñā. How is this so? In this sutra, wherever all dharmas are concerned, it repeatedly says "is not" and "is named," in order to make clear that marks exist while the nature is empty, intending to have people contemplate the fundamental emptiness and at once attain liberation. Those of sharp faculties can hear one and understand ten; they awaken to the fact that the view of self and the rest are likewise marks existing while the nature is empty, and so with a single blade they cut straight in and sever its root on the spot. But now it says the Buddha speaks of a view of self and the rest. That such a one leans stubbornly to the side of existing marks, unable to penetrate that the views of self, person, and so on are likewise fundamentally empty, is thereby made clear. Hence it says he does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata.

"Buddha" is spoken in terms of marks. "Tathāgata" is spoken in terms of nature. Above it says "the Buddha speaks of a view of self"; then it says "does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata." This precisely reveals that such a person, regarding the view of self and the rest, knows only the meaning that marks exist and has not understood the meaning that the nature is empty. If so, then the views of self, person, and the rest can never be removed. An ancient worthy once asked his master to untie his bonds. The master said: "Who bound you?" The scripture of this section precisely makes this meaning clear. You should understand that the substance of the nature is empty and still, and fundamentally has no bonds. Now to set a view of self, person, and the rest across the mind, and to say the Buddha also spoke thus — is this not spinning a cocoon around oneself? Therefore our World-Honored One, out of unconditioned compassion and the pity of one substance, especially gave rise to this whole section of scripture on behalf of the Elder. It is to enable all living beings to see through directly the mind-source that is fundamentally without self and without views, and so to attain the ultimate untying of bonds and removal of attachment. The importance of this section's meaning is thereby made clear. What is that meaning? Listen to what follows.
(Zi) Next, explaining and establishing the reason.

"Why is this? What the World-Honored One speaks of as the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a being, and the view of a life is not the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a being, and the view of a life; therefore it is named the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a being, and the view of a life."

Wherever the sutra says "is named," it is always spoken in terms of marks, that is, in terms of the meaning of dependent arising. Wherever it says "is not," it is always spoken in terms of nature, that is, in terms of the meaning that the nature is empty. You should understand that when the Buddha says "the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a being, the view of a life," his intention is to have people realize that the views of self, person, and the rest are all illusory marks of dependent arising. If one can know illusion, one is at once apart from it — where then is the view of self? His intention is also to have people realize that the views of self, person, and the rest are fundamentally not the empty and still nature of awareness. Then, being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened — where then is the view of self to be left behind? This is the true meaning of the Buddha's speaking of the view of self. To say now that the Buddha spoke of a view of self while being unaware of anything else carries in its tone a mind brooding over it — this very thing is clinging to the real. He wished to have them break their clinging, and now they have added one more clinging: how can the view of self be left behind? And even if they could leave it behind, to retain the thought of a "one who leaves" and a "that which is left" is still the view of self. How can its roots be pulled out completely? Hence it says he does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathāgata.

To say that this person does not understand is precisely to have students deeply grasp and understand on the mind-source that is fundamentally pure and without self and without views. Here the text does not say "the Buddha speaks" or "the Tathāgata speaks," but deliberately says "the World-Honored One speaks," and there is an especially fine meaning in this. To say "Buddha" would lean to the side of marks; to say "Tathāgata" would omit the side of cultivation. The meaning here is precisely to have people awaken to and contemplate the fundamentally empty nature so as to undertake cultivation. And "World-Honored One" is the general title among the ten epithets, encompassing within it the meanings of both Buddha and Tathāgata. Hence it is deliberately brought up to reveal the meaning. The sense is that the meaning here is the secret transmission of mind from one who is complete in the ten epithets. That the World-Honored One is honored by the world lies precisely in this. One must cultivate in accordance with this meaning; only then may one, with the cause perfected and the fruit fulfilled, become a Buddha, and with cultivation perfected and the nature revealed, realize the Tathāgata. Why is this? The view of self is the root of ignorance and the cause of becoming an ordinary being. Breaking the view of self is the light of wisdom and the road to becoming a holy one. And the meaning made clear here is precisely the diamond sword of wisdom that breaks the view of self and can sever its roots. Without relying on this method, the view of self is not easily removed; and even if removed, it cannot be removed entirely. In short, what is said here is precisely the direct instruction for practice. To take it merely as a piece of metaphysical reasoning would be the greatest possible betrayal of the Buddha's kindness.

It was said above that "is not the view of self, therefore it is named the view of self" must not be taken merely as a principle for contemplating emptiness; it is the supreme practice for breaking the view of self, directly pointed out. And in speaking of practice, there is an extremely important meaning that must be understood first. Hitherto it seems no one has analyzed this point. I must now distinguish it layer by layer and make each point clear. Then not only will the practice in this section and in this sutra gain its essentials; in all scriptures, whatever is said about nature, cultivation, and the categories of practice will not fail to be kept in order. And the various faults of clinging to nature while discarding cultivation, or letting affairs obstruct principle, may likewise be avoided.

In all the dharmas the Buddha taught, there are no more than two meanings: making clear the nature, and making clear cultivation. Moreover, in a single sentence of Dharma, when he speaks of nature he must also include cultivation, and when he speaks of cultivation he also embraces nature. If one does not understand it in this way, one remains forever outside the gate of the Buddha-Dharma.

Now nature means the principle-nature; cultivation means the work of cultivation. The principle-nature should be seen as equal within differences; the work of cultivation should be seen as differentiated within equality. What does it mean to see equality within differences? It means one should understand that the Buddha's teachings often explain the principle through one matter, and that this principle in fact runs through all matters. If one who hears the Dharma does not understand this pervasiveness, then one sees only differences and does not see equality; how could one observe the principle and realize the nature? (Because the nature is equal, the principle must be equal.) For instance, in this sutra there are very many places saying "is not" and "is named." The hearer should grasp that the principle within them is fundamentally without duality. For wherever it says "is not," it is spoken in terms of the nature, the substance of principle, to make clear that it is fundamentally empty. Wherever it says "is named," it is spoken in terms of the marks that arise from conditions, to make clear that they are illusory existents. And wherever "is not" and "is named" are spoken together, it is always to make clear that nature and marks are neither one nor different. To speak in this way is intended to make one know that whoever wishes to realize the dharma-nature should, with respect to the marks of dharmas, understand that they are not one and so not cling, and also understand that they are not different and so not annihilate. Hence this principle is not a matter of differences but of equality.

In other words, this is not so of one dharma alone but of every dharma. That is, whatever the dharma, one should understand this principle clearly, not settle on either extreme, and merge back into the equal substance of the nature. But if one discusses the work of cultivation in terms of the meaning of "is not" and "is named," then there are great differences. One cannot, just because the principle-nature is equal, be vague and muddled and treat everything as one and the same. Were it so, one would inevitably take the meaning spoken by the Buddha as mere reasoning about emptiness, supposing that it is only meant to have people contemplate everything as empty. Because such a person does not know how to carefully realize the differences within equality, he naturally has no way to set his hand to it, and so does not know that this is the direct instruction for practice. Or again, not knowing that it is an instruction for practice, one supposes it to be the Tathāgata's own realm, which we ordinary people would not presume to discuss. Hence those who fear prajñā are very many indeed. This is in fact the reason why this sutra has through the ages mostly been expounded only as a semblance of prajñā. And those more extreme still cultivate not a single dharma and do not remove the view of self either, but instead congratulate themselves, saying: I study prajñā. It is precisely such people who are meant by the term "madness." All such illnesses come from never having carefully distinguished and clearly separated the relation between nature and cultivation and the categories of practice — in other words, equality within difference and difference within equality. This is why I cannot but now analyze it minutely and explain it in detail.

The categories of cultivation practice are too many to enumerate. But they can be summarized as two. (1) The gate of contemplation, also called principle-contemplation. (2) The gate of practice, also called cultivation in affairs.

Principle-contemplation means relying on the principle-nature taught by the Buddha that can run through all things, and applying deep realization and strict enlightened contemplation to it. Only thus can one apply it to the gate of practice. From this one can know that what is called principle-contemplation, though it is principle, has already appeared in cultivation; and though it is cultivation, it still belongs to principle. Therefore it is wrong to regard principle-contemplation as a slow, secondary undertaking; and it is also wrong to regard it as sufficient cultivation in itself. Since ancient times, who knows how many have fallen into this fault. In short, in doing principle-contemplation one must also cultivate in affairs; and in cultivating in affairs one must also do principle-contemplation. Lacking either, one cannot speak of the work of cultivation.

Cultivation in affairs includes giving, keeping precepts, and even reading scriptures, reciting the Buddha's name, raising a hand, bowing the head — whatever appears in action and behavior, great or small, fine or coarse, is all included. Its method of cultivation must deal with each affair on its own terms. Affairs have thousands upon thousands of differences, and the methods of cultivation therefore have thousands upon thousands of differences too. For example, bowing has the rules of bowing, and chanting has the rules of chanting — how could they all be one and the same?

Nor is that all. Since principle-contemplation reaches through to cultivation in affairs, when one practices principle-contemplation one should not only rely on the principle-nature described above and contemplate its equal principle; one should also, in accordance with the kind of affair being cultivated, contemplate its differentiated principle. If one knows only how to contemplate equality and not difference, or knows only how to contemplate difference and not equality, then it is as good as blind cultivation. You should understand that nature, cultivation, the principle within cultivation, and affairs can neither be split into two separate pieces nor muddled into one. One must realize the non-difference within difference and the difference within non-difference. Only then can nature and cultivation be non-dual and principle and affairs perfectly interfused. For there must be orderly arrangement within perfect interfusion, and perfect interfusion within orderly arrangement. Only then is it true interfusion and true non-duality, and no cultivation will fail to succeed. This is the first essential for one who studies Buddhism. If one cannot realize these points clearly, then one is merely plausible but wrong, and will certainly achieve nothing.

Take, for example, "is not" and "is named." Some passages speak in terms of the six pāramitās, others in terms of adorning Buddha-lands. But adorning Buddha-lands refers precisely to cultivating the practices of the six pāramitās, and can be regarded as belonging to the same class as those that speak in terms of the six pāramitās. There are also passages that speak in terms of the thirty-two marks and the complete body marks, and others that speak in terms of worlds and dust-motes. All of these are marks of objects. Yet although they are all marks of objects, if one distinguishes them finely, they cannot be treated as one and the same class. For the thirty-two marks and the complete body marks are brought about by cultivating merit and wisdom, whereas worlds and dust-motes need not be cultivated at all. Hence with worlds and dust-motes there is no cultivation in affairs to speak of; one need only practice principle-contemplation, contemplating the equal principle-nature and not clinging to either existence or emptiness. But the thirty-two marks and the rest should be assigned to the class of the six pāramitās. On the one hand, contemplate the principle-nature that is illusory yet fundamentally empty; on the other hand, contemplate the six pāramitās as the essential gate for saving oneself and saving others. Body marks and Buddha-lands are absolutely indispensable for drawing in living beings. Although they are illusory and fundamentally empty, one should simply not cling to them; one must never annihilate the affairs themselves. As for applying them in action, one must follow the illusory Dharma and cultivate diligently without slackening. This is what is meant by setting up a practice hall like a moon in water and carrying on the Buddha's work in a dream. One need only not retain in the mind any thought of a cultivator or a cultivation. This is the work of cultivation that practices the six pāramitās and the rest in terms of the meaning of "is not" and "is named."

With the view of self, however, it is quite otherwise. The six pāramitās and the rest are matters that should be accomplished, whereas the view of self and the rest are matters that should be dissolved away — the exact opposite. Therefore, although contemplating the equal principle-nature that is illusory yet fundamentally empty is the same as in cultivating the six pāramitās, when one contemplates in terms of the affair, one should contemplate that it is wholly not existing as nature but merely a provisional name. In the mind there must not remain the slightest self or the slightest view. And as for applying it in action, one should keep far from the names and marks of illusory existence and deeply illumine the mind-nature that is fundamentally empty. This is the work of cultivation that removes the view of self in terms of the meaning of "is not" and "is named." Knowing this, one can by analogy understand the cultivation that dissolves all matters of ignorance, affliction, and the rest. You should understand that the view of self is deep-rooted and firmly fixed. If one wishes now to remove it, without relying on the cultivation described here one certainly cannot remove it. Let me first state its outline. Once the outline is clear, one can then investigate it layer by layer, for the principle of the cultivation described here is exceedingly fine.

Why is it said that if one wishes to remove the view of self, one cannot do so except by this method? The principle has been spoken of before, but I fear it has not yet been thoroughly understood. Let me now put it in other words to make it clear.

Suppose there is someone who knows the harm of the view of self and resolves to remove it. But if in his mind he sees the view of self as hard to remove, then he has already taken the view of self to be truly existing. With one view that the view of self truly exists lodged in his mind, and another view of removing the view of self lodged beside it, he adds bond upon bond — how can the view of self be removed? Why is this? So long as there remains in the mind the faintest trace of a remover and a removed, it is still a view and still a clinging to self.

Therefore our World-Honored One especially teaches here to illumine directly the mind-source that is fundamentally without self and without views. Then not only is the view of self absent, but the view of no-self is absent as well. And so the view of self leaves not even a trace. What could be more direct and satisfying than this? I would not presume to claim that I can remove the view of self, but on this matter I have long and unbroken experience and contemplation. Let me briefly set out one or two of its twists and hidden subtleties. I know well that the cultivation here is subtle and essential. Wishing now that all of you may gain at once, and not daring to betray this section of scripture, I shall respectfully unfold, so far as I can grasp it, the cultivation made clear in the sutra, drawing it out in full, so that those with the heart for it may understand it thoroughly. Perhaps the prajñā Dharma-door may thereby be greatly clarified in the world. This is my humble wish. Yet the flavor of its meaning is deep and profound, and to explain it is not easy. Unless one quiets the mind and settles the breath, it will surely not be easy to grasp either. I hope all of you will ponder it well.

Let me first take the meaning of "is not" and trace it to its source and to its end, making clear that it is the most wonderful cultivation for removing the view of self. Now the view of self is what is called the root of ignorance. You should understand that the pure self-nature fundamentally has no ignorance. Yet ordinary beings, because they do not penetrate the one true dharma-realm, from beginningless time have moved without awareness, and so it has continued to this day. Within their minds, from inside out, there is nothing but pitch-black ignorance. The light of the nature that is inherently present has long since been hidden and no longer appears. This is what is meant by "the unborn-and-unceasing joined with the arising-and-ceasing is named consciousness." Since the whole of one is buried in a pitch-black barrel with not a shred of light, to speak of not clinging is itself clinging; to have one contemplate emptiness, what he contemplates is precisely the sentiment of consciousness and not the emptiness of nature. Therefore the single phrase "is not the view of self" does not merely have one contemplate and observe the emptiness of nature. It is to teach one to rouse the spirit, resolutely and decisively, and with all one's might kick the view of self and the rest headlong. At the root, one does not acknowledge that there is any such view of self, person, and the rest within the self-nature. The two words "is not" should be understood in this way. This is the first and most excellent skillful means.

It was said above that with the whole of one buried in ignorance, to speak of not clinging is itself clinging. Then to speak of not acknowledging must likewise be the working of the sentiment of consciousness — how then can it be called a most excellent skillful means? You should understand that ordinary beings have from beginningless time taken the thief for their son for so long. Now, instructed by the Buddha, they come to know that he is not, and are willing not to acknowledge him. Since they both know and are willing, the "unborn-and-unceasing joined with arising-and-ceasing" shows a great crack. This very fact means that from within the shell of ignorance a single thread of the light of wisdom has appeared. This is initial enlightenment. This is the first step of turning the back on dust and joining with enlightenment. If this is not a most excellent skillful means, what is?

In short, a thing that has been cemented and fixed for so long — if one does not first break with it in this way, how could one suddenly be free of it? Therefore the two words "is not" in the text require great effort. It is not merely a matter of contemplating in this way.

Question: If one contemplates with enlightenment in this way, then the joined-together does indeed show a great crack. That is true. But it only shows a crack. What further skillful means should be used if one wishes ignorance to be gone altogether?

Answer: Use this very method, and ignorance is gone on the spot. There is no need to seek further skillful means. Hence it is said: knowing illusion, one is at once apart from it, without resorting to skillful means. Otherwise, what would be so wonderful about it? You should understand that although the self-nature is pure and there are confused and tangled deluded thoughts of ignorance, the view of self, and the rest, the self-nature itself is ever constant and unchanging, pure as it is. For the self-nature is the real substance, while ignorance is an illusory mark. The one real and the one illusory, though from beginningless time they have been joined into one, are in fact joined outwardly and not inwardly, and fundamentally do not correspond. It is like the Jing and Wei rivers, clearly distinct and each not mingling with the other. This principle only the Buddha Tathāgata, who has realized the ultimate enlightenment, can know thoroughly. Hence in the Mahāyāna scriptures this principle is frequently spoken to instruct ordinary beings, because all ordinary beings use it daily without knowing it.

And the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment states this principle most clearly. It says: "This ignorance has no real substance. It is like a man in a dream: while dreaming, it is not nothing; but when he wakes, there is nothing to be found at all." The dream illustrates the delusion of living beings; the waking illustrates the awakening of the practitioner. One who studies Buddhism must first believe this. What is called "faith is the gate of entry to the path" means firmly believing the principle spoken by the Buddha, so that in entering the path one finds its gate. For ordinary beings have never known this principle from the first. Though they know it now, without true cultivation it will still be hard to understand at once. And without faith, where is the place of entry? Therefore, when one hears that "is not the view of self," one should straightway accord with and enter the mind-source that is fundamentally pure.

"Straightway" means to cast everything aside and pay it no heed, and alone, by oneself, to contemplate with enlightenment directly at the place where no thought has yet stirred. This is like having long taken a thief for one's son, so that the guest has long since usurped the master. Now, fortunately, one knows that he is a thief — how could one go on casting glances at him and tangling with him? Still less need one worry that his power is great and hard to remove. If one worries, one only fans his flames. You must know that he has no root at all. His former power came entirely from one's own trust in him. Now that one knows he is not, and withholds trust, he has no way to exert himself and must submit and be converted. Why fear him? This is the foremost essential for removing delusion. Do not neglect it.

Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: knowing illusion, one is at once apart from it. The word "knowing" is most wonderful. Knowing is precisely enlightened contemplation. If one can contemplate with enlightenment, the view melts like ice. It is like a rat peering greedily into a dark corner: if it is caught in the light of awareness, it flees of itself. So it is here. For two thoughts cannot arise at the same time. The arising of deluded mind comes precisely from the slackening of right mindfulness. When right mindfulness is roused, deluded thoughts are gone. This is a natural principle, not something strange. Hence it says "at once apart." You should understand that "at once apart" and "knowing illusion" are from the first not two things. This is the most direct and most essential method for removing delusion. It must not be taken lightly. Contemplate with enlightenment in this way at all times, without the least indulgence, and from where could the view of self arise? Even if it arose, its strength would be very weak. When the work is mature after a long time, it will naturally not arise at all. This is the cultivation of "is not the view of self."

There is something that should be added. Ordinary beings, from beginningless time without awareness, have never let their deluded thoughts pause for a moment. If one now wishes to know illusion and contemplate with enlightenment, one must first practice preparatory skillful means. Otherwise, how could one know it as illusion and contemplate it with enlightenment? For example, one who has long lived in a noisy marketplace, with clamor day and night without cease, does not notice the noise. But in a quiet and leisurely place, the slightest faint sound is noticed. So it is here. One must first firmly keep the precepts in order to cut off defiling conditions, and read the Mahāyāna widely in order to understand Buddhist principle. Let this mind gain a little quiet, and let worldly views gradually lighten. Only then can one know illusion and contemplate with enlightenment.

That "is not the view of self" is placed last in this sutra carries this same meaning. Yet although it is spoken last, in cultivation it should come first. If one has not gained the essentials of the method for removing ignorance and the view of self, then how can one thoroughly illumine the nature, cultivation, principle, and affairs spoken of since the opening of the sutra? One would fail to grasp the essentials of all of them. This principle must certainly not go unknown.

The cultivation of "is named the view of self" and the rest is even more important and even more wonderful. If one knows only "is not" and not "is named," how can the view of self be completely purified? I hope all of you will first realize the meaning of "is not the view of self" for a while, and then listen to the meaning of "is named the view of self." In hearing the Dharma, what matters is that every single word be deeply realized in the heart. Otherwise one hears as if one had not heard, and what benefit is there?

Now I shall set forth the cultivation of "is named the view of self." Someone may ask: wherever this sutra says "is named," it always makes clear the meaning of not annihilating. But the view of self is something that should be dissolved away. How does this fit? The cultivation of "is not," spoken of before, was a resolute break with it, in order to break its cemented and fixed sentiment. I already know that it is wonderful. Now you say that "is named" is likewise a most wonderful and most essential cultivation — does one both break with it and draw it back? Answer: that is not what is meant. It was said above that affairs differ, and the cultivation therefore differs accordingly. This refers precisely to the sentence "is named the view of self." Since you already know that the view of self is something to be dissolved away, why do you confuse it with the principle-contemplation and cultivation in affairs that should be accomplished, and make idle talk of it?

You should understand that the meaning of "is named the view of self" is to make clear that the view of self is an illusory mark manifested by the true nature. What is called dissolving away does not mean annihilating the self-nature; it means removing only the disease, not removing the dharma. This is the first point. It further makes clear that the view of self is a dharma arising from conditions: if the mind grasps at conditions, the view of self arises along with conditions; if the mind does not arise, the view of self has no way to arise. This is what is meant by knowing illusion, one is at once apart from it; being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened. This is the second point. These two meanings are exceedingly important. For the cultivation that removes the view of self, nothing is more wonderful than this. Without relying on it, one can never remove it. I fear you still do not understand, so I shall speak further in detail. Listen attentively, listen attentively.

Let me first make clear the first meaning. The views of self, person, and the rest are precisely discrimination and clinging. They are what are called the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Consciousness is nothing else: it is the defiled mark that the true nature, because of non-awakening, manifests in accord with defiling conditions. This is what is meant by the unborn-and-unceasing joined with arising-and-ceasing. Now, to contemplate the meaning of "is not" and break with it is simply not to join with it, so that it dissolves into nothing. If it dissolves, then the discriminating sixth consciousness is precisely wonderful observing wisdom, and the clinging seventh consciousness is precisely the wisdom of equality. How could they be annihilated? All ordinary beings have suffered from non-awakening, not knowing it as consciousness, and mistaking it for the true nature. Hence it is said: taking a thief for one's son. You should understand that this thief is not an outsider but a thief of the house, and moreover a principal figure. To break with him now is meant to make him turn from evil and return to the right. It is like an only son whom one disowns because he will not attend to his duties — the intent is truly to hope he will turn back. If one were simply to cast him off forever, the house too would be destroyed. So it is here. One must not, because one hates ignorance and the view of self, fail to spare the vase while throwing at the rat, and so walk the road of reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing wisdom. The non-thought of the non-Buddhists and the sinking into emptiness and stagnation of stillness of the Two Vehicles both suffer from this fault. They do not realize that having leaned to emptiness, the mind still grasps. If the mind grasps marks, then one is attached to self, person, being, and life. How then can the view of self ever be removed?

Let me further make clear the second meaning. Considering what was said under the first meaning — that at first, because of non-awakening, one took ignorance for the true nature — now that one knows this and does not acknowledge it, one can see that this very single thought is precisely awakening. Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened, and there are no gradual stages. First contemplate the meaning of "is not": since one can know illusion, one is at once apart from it. One need only continue this knowing, and when conditions come the mind does not arise, and so the one mind is pure. This is why being apart from illusion is at once awakening. What is called being apart means not arising. At first there may indeed be some forcing, but when the work is mature after a long time it will naturally not arise. When it naturally does not arise, the view of self is ultimately purified. You should understand that this meaning makes clear that when it does not arise, it simply does not arise, straight through. In other words, not arising is enough. There is no need to further discriminate whether or not it has arisen. Why? Because discrimination is precisely grasping at conditions, and so the mind has arisen again. This is ignorance. This is the view of self. In short, in the work of removing delusion what matters is a single clean cut. The least glance aside and it is a lotus root cut but its fibers still joined — a great taboo, a great taboo. On this meaning the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment has eight more lines that state it most thoroughly, and they can illuminate our sutra in turn.

The sutra says: "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. Toward all deluded minds, do not suppress them either. Dwelling in the realm of deluded thinking, do not add knowing. Toward that non-knowing, do not discriminate the real." These eight lines of the sutra, from ancient times to the present, have been explained differently by each according to his own insight, so that every person's account differs. Let me now explain their meaning thoroughly, without one hooded or covered phrase. You should understand that among the eight lines, the first two are the master, and the two words "do not give rise" are the master. The six lines that follow unfold and explain the meaning in turn, to make clear the reason why there is no arising. It is saying that only thus is it a true non-arising.

In short, the six lines that follow are not only a footnote to the first two; they are precisely a most wonderful footnote to "being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened." The deluded mind is deluded thought, and refers precisely to discrimination, clinging, and the rest of ignorance. You should understand that the deluded mind is nothing else: it is the whole of the real manifesting in accord with defilement. How could it be suppressed? One must not mistake non-arising of thought for being like a withered tree or dead ashes. When one is apart from illusion, one is at once awakened, and then the whole of delusion is the real — why suppress it? If one suppresses it, then jade and stone are burned together, and that is not the true meaning of non-arising. Hence it says: toward all deluded minds, do not suppress them either. Nor may one mistake "do not suppress" for dwelling in the realm of deluded thinking. You should understand that there is only consciousness, no realm. Since deluded thoughts no longer arise, how could there be a realm? How could there be dwelling? For being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened, and then all is empty. Why add knowing whether or not one dwells in a realm? If one adds knowing, that is putting a head on top of a head, and thought has arisen again. How can that be called non-arising? Hence it says: dwelling in the realm of deluded thinking, do not add knowing.

Nor may one further mistake this: if there is no knowing at all, would one not fall into blankness? You should understand that since one does not suppress, it is not the same as a withered tree or dead ashes.
