Therefore when thought does not arise, the numinous light shines alone, utterly free of the senses and their objects. Hence it is said: being apart from illusion, one is at once awakened. For awakening is the real nature. Why need one further identify whether or not it is real? If one identifies it, that is the ordinary person troubling himself for nothing, and can it still be called non-arising? Hence it says: toward that non-knowing, do not discriminate the real.

The overall meaning of these six lines is simply to draw out the meaning of the passage above in that sutra: that having illumination and having awareness are both named obstructions. The meaning of "is named the view of self" in our sutra is likewise so. Now since the view of self arises from conditions, one can see that within the self-nature it is fundamentally unborn; it is only an illusory mark arising in accord with conditions. It follows that the view of self is the name, and the true nature is the reality. Now that one knows it is fundamentally not the substance of the true nature but an illusory mark, and illumines directly the mind-source in which the illusory mark was fundamentally never born — where then is the provisional name? Where does the illusory mark remain? The student should in this way use the sharp knife that cuts through tangled hemp, with a single clean cut. Then deluded conditions do not arise. Not arising is enough; there is nothing to be apart from, and no one who is apart; nothing to illumine, and no one who illumines. For that being apart and that illumining are likewise provisional names and illusory marks of opposition arising from conditions, and in the pure self-nature they are fundamentally nonexistent.

But if, having known that it is not and being apart from it, one anxiously discriminates whether or not one is already apart, or joyfully declares that one can be apart, then one is still clinging to it as truly existing, and has not yet clearly understood the meaning that the name is not real. This is clinging to dharmas. This is the view of self. Hence one who is good at practice must be apart all the way through, and when cutting, cut at once. This is the cultivation of "is named the view of self." From what has been said above, one can know that the cultivation described in this section is most wonderful and most essential. Why?

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment has another essential passage: "All Buddhas, from the original ground of their initial resolve, rely throughout on perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-way." The cultivation here is precisely perfect illumination of the mark of pure enlightenment. Hence ignorance and the view of self are cut off once and forever. Is it not wonderful? Is it not essential? Hitherto everyone has read this section merely as empty principle — a great mistake. One should urgently understand it in this way. And one must not merely know it and stop there, like entering a mountain of treasures and returning empty-handed. One should urgently cultivate in accordance with it and so gain its benefit.

You should understand that the true nature has long been obstructed by ignorance and the view of self. Without breaking this obstruction, how can one see the nature? And if one does not see the nature, how can one transcend the ordinary and enter the holy? Nor is that all. From the opening of the sutra one is told to make great vows and undertake great practices, and the intent is to break the self. Yet the view of self is deep-rooted, and unless one can bring effort to bear precisely on breaking the self, great vows and great practices may not suddenly be brought forth either. Observe that this sutra begins with great vows and great practices and concludes with breaking the view of self. Head and tail answer to each other, precisely indicating that the way to perfect the beginning and the end, to transcend the ordinary and enter the holy, lies entirely in this. One should understand it thus and advance on both fronts at once.

There is, besides, an essential meaning that must not go unknown. This section, explaining in terms of the view of self that detachment too is to be detached from, is precisely to reveal the meaning of neither defiled nor pure. (The first section made clear neither arising nor ceasing; the next made clear neither increasing nor decreasing; this one makes clear neither defiled nor pure. Together they make clear the empty mark of all dharmas. The meaning is exactly the same as in the Heart Sutra.) The view of self is defilement; being apart from the view of self is purity. Yet to speak of defilement and purity is still a mark of opposition. But the purity of the pure self-nature is absolute. Absolute means that both defilement and purity are absent. Therefore, in being apart from the view of self, the being-apart too should be left behind. If one retains a remover and a removed, one still falls into the marks of opposition and is not the absolute nature. Then the view of self is in the end not completely purified. Hence this section teaches that in breaking the self one must not do it twig by twig and joint by joint. One should straightway accord with and enter the place where not one thought arises. Then the defilement of the view of self, being a provisional name and fundamentally nonexistent, and so the purity of being apart from the view of self is likewise left far behind. Why? Since there is no defilement, how could there be purity? When defilement and purity are both left behind, that is true purity.

Of the three sections under the empty mark of all dharmas, the first explains the meaning in terms of the body, the second explains it in terms of the world, and this one explains it in terms of the deluded mind. The view of self is the deluded mind. Together these three sections precisely reveal that body, mind, and world are nothing but illusion, and that all empty marks are by nature equal.

Furthermore. Ordinary beings cling to the body as self and to the world as belonging to the self. Both self and what belongs to the self arise from views. Hence body and world are what is clung to, and views are what clings. The meaning of the three sections is to make clear that the marks of both the clinging and the clung-to are empty, and that even the thought of an emptiness and of what is emptied is empty as well. This is what is called the empty mark of all dharmas. It is also to draw out the meaning that no mark of dharma is born and that the marks of dharmas are fundamentally nonexistent. Hence the section below concludes with the words about no mark of dharma being born.

The whole sutra, with its thousands of words, is nothing but for the sake of breaking the four marks of self, person, being, and life. And marks arise from views. At this point it explains that the view of self and the rest are provisional names arising from conditions and are fundamentally empty by nature. This meaning is precisely what sums up the whole sutra. For this sutra was spoken originally to break the self. Now it draws out the breaking of the self to its ultimate point. This is where all the meanings of the whole sutra converge.

It was said above: the bodhisattva penetrates selflessness and the selflessness of dharmas. And again: knowing that all dharmas are selfless, one attains patient acceptance. Here it goes further still, to the very ultimate. Why? Accord with and enter the place of non-arising, and the view of self is fundamentally nonexistent. How could there first be a self and then its absence? And how could there be any patient acceptance to attain? The bodhisattva should penetrate thoroughly in this way, and only then is it ultimate selflessness and ultimate attainment of patient acceptance. Hence the section below concludes with: one who has resolved for supreme bodhi should, with respect to all dharmas, thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand, and not give rise to marks of dharmas, since marks of dharmas are fundamentally nonexistent. A bodhisattva is one who has resolved for the supreme mind. Penetrating is knowing, seeing, believing, and understanding. The meaning runs straight through to the beginning of the sutra. What was said at the beginning — that one should thus subdue one's mind and should abide as instructed — is nothing else: it is to enable one to realize that the marks of all dharmas are fundamentally unborn. And so the meaning of the whole sutra is gathered up without a drop escaping, complete and without remainder.
(Ren) Next, concluding with non-arising. This is divided into two: (Gui) first, directly making clear non-arising; next, that non-arising too is nonexistent.
(Gui) First, directly making clear non-arising.
"Subhūti, one who has resolved for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi should, with respect to all dharmas, thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand, and not give rise to marks of dharmas."

"One who has resolved for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi" answers precisely to the phrase "all bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas" at the opening of the sutra. That is to say, the bodhisattva who has resolved for the great mind should thus know, see, believe, and understand. What has been spoken since the opening of the sutra — resolving for the vast mind, undertaking vast practices, not grasping the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas, and even not dwelling in the resolving mind, not dwelling in the speaking of Dharma, not dwelling in the attaining of fruit, and not dwelling even in non-dwelling — is nothing but to have one know, see, believe, and understand in precisely this way. For only by thus knowing, seeing, believing, and understanding can one penetrate selflessness and the selflessness of dharmas. Hence it says: one should thus know, see, believe, and understand.

Since the opening of the latter half, the text has spoken only of "resolving for bodhi" and not of the word "mind," and this is in order to dispel the view that clings to this as being the bodhi-mind. If one clings to a dharma, one falls into the four marks of self, person, being, and life, and it is not the bodhi-mind; hence it must be dispelled. At this point all dharmas are empty marks, and the bodhi-mind is present before one. Hence here it does not say "resolving for bodhi" but "resolving for the bodhi-mind." "One should thus know, see, believe, and understand, and not give rise to marks of dharmas" is precisely to show that one who resolves for the bodhi-mind must be thus; only thus is it the bodhi-mind. This also concludes the earlier meaning of dispelling and sweeping away the resolving mind so that it does not dwell. It is to have one open this kind of knowing and seeing, give rise to this kind of believing and understanding, and not give rise to marks of dharmas. How could it be to have one not resolve for the bodhi-mind?

With this one conclusion, everything said before is fully set forth in all its meaning, all its veins and channels run through at once, and its spirit is perfectly complete. It is like painting a dragon and then dotting the eye, so that it flies away. As for the writing, it too is most marvellous. "All dharmas" refers broadly to the mundane and the supramundane, to realms, practices, and fruits. It includes everything said above: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas; body marks and the thirty-two marks; and even the realms of worlds and dust-motes; the great vows and great practices of giving and keeping precepts, for the sake of widely saving living beings and adorning Buddha-lands; and even the practices of being apart from marks, apart from thoughts, and apart from the view of self; the gaining of true faith, the arising of the true mark, the accomplishment of the first and rarest, the supreme and foremost and rarest; and also the attaining of merit, the attaining of virtue, the attaining of patient acceptance, being named a srota-āpanna, and even being named a bodhisattva, being named a Buddha, and being named anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. All are gathered in at once. The two words "thus" refer precisely to all the various meanings spoken above. And the meanings spoken above are no more than arising from conditions and empty by nature.

And in the final major section, which investigates non-dwelling to the utmost in order to accomplish realization, the first section, making clear the equal dharma-realm and revealing the accomplishment of the selflessness of dharmas, investigates to the utmost the meaning that emptiness of nature does not hinder dependent arising. Because emptiness of nature does not hinder dependent arising, the equal dharma-realm is accomplished. The next section, on the empty mark of all dharmas, concluding with the non-arising of dharmas, investigates to the utmost the meaning that dependent arising does not hinder emptiness of nature. Because dependent arising does not hinder emptiness of nature, in the very midst of all dharmas there is the empty mark.

Seen in this light, the flavor of the two words "thus" is precisely to reveal that all dharmas are one such and that all is so. Because all is one such, to know, see, believe, and understand in this way is not to give rise to marks of dharmas. Otherwise, the marks of dharmas are not annihilated at all — how could one say they do not arise? It can be seen that what is called non-arising proceeds precisely from "thus." It does not mean that non-arising is taken as non-arising in the sense of final annihilation. Hence the text below expresses it with "is not the marks of dharmas, therefore it is named the marks of dharmas." One should thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand. This is what is called the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment. Ponder it carefully.

The three words "know," "see," and "understand" are in their basic meaning not greatly different. Yet when the three are said in sequence, each has its own reference, and there are great distinctions. They must not be regarded vaguely as one. There are many such constructions in the Buddhist scriptures. In every case one should distinguish their flavor and understand what each refers to. One must certainly not be content with a shallow reading and pass over them, or even suppose the words to be redundant — that would be a great mistake.

What then do these three words refer to? Jiaxiang says that knowing is the wisdom of the worldly truth and seeing is the wisdom of the ultimate truth. Datian says that knowing is inferential cognition and seeing is direct perception. I would say one should follow Asaṅga's treatise. The treatise says: "Wisdom relying on śamatha is knowing. Relying on vipaśyanā is seeing. Both of these relying on samādhi is understanding." This meaning makes clear that all three are wisdom; only because the skillful means they rely on differ are three names established.

Śamatha is here rendered as "calming." Calming means concentration. Wisdom born from concentration is called knowing. From this it is clear that knowing is the wisdom of the ultimate truth. In concentration all conditions are stilled, and one knows with perfect clarity. Hence it is called knowing. This accords exactly with the earlier meaning in this sutra, where the mind of the three periods is unattainable and all dharmas, arising from conditions, are empty — opening the Buddha's right knowing. For knowing is spoken from the side of inner realization.

Vipaśyanā is here rendered as "observing." Observing is precisely insight. Wisdom issuing from insight is called seeing. From this it is clear that seeing is the wisdom of the worldly truth. With insight, all differentiated marks of affairs are seen through without exception. Hence it is called seeing. This is exactly the same as the earlier meaning in this sutra, where the five eyes, the sands of the Ganges, and not clinging to oneness or difference open the Buddha's perfect seeing. For seeing is spoken from the side of outward illumination.
